query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In as-received Q235 steel, the native oxide film that naturally develops acts as a protective barrier under high-temperature (700–900 °C) salt exposures by forming a denser and more adherent scale, while at room temperature its defect-rich nature fails to sufficiently inhibit corrosive attack.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its as-received state, with its naturally formed oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples: one set with the native oxide layer intact (or thermally pre-formed for controlled oxide characteristics) and a reference set that is freshly polished to remove the oxide.
generation.conditions: Exposure to a corrosive environment consisting of a 75% Na2SO4 and 25% NaCl salt mixture at room temperature and at 700–900 °C under controlled annealing conditions to promote reproducible oxide formation and composition.
generation.structural_mediator: The composition, thickness, and defect density of the native oxide film acting as the mediator between the metal substrate and the aggressive environment.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, accelerated oxidation kinetics promote the formation of a more stable, dense oxide scale that withstands salt-induced corrosion. At room temperature, however, the incompletely developed or defect-laden native oxide allows localized breakdown, leading to higher corrosion rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature salt exposure, samples with the controlled pre-formed oxide film will exhibit lower corrosion rates (evidenced by reduced mass loss and fewer spallation events) compared to freshly polished samples; at room temperature, differences will be minimal or the oxide film may even promote localized corrosion due to its inherent defects.
generation.baseline: Performance comparisons will be made against untreated Q235 steel and a benchmark alloy such as 304 stainless steel known for its stable corrosion-resistant oxide.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies exclusively under the defined conditions of a 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl environment at room temperature and 700–900 °C. Variations in salt composition, exposure duration, or thermal history may alter oxide formation and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact chemical makeup and defect distribution within the native oxide film on Q235 steel, and how variations in these parameters might affect its protective behavior across different temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled study using two groups of Q235 steel samples: one group retains its native oxide layer (or is thermally pre-treated to form a controlled oxide), and the other group is freshly polished to remove the oxide. Expose both groups along with a 304 stainless steel reference to a 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl environment at room temperature and at 800 °C for a fixed period. Analyze the oxide layers before and after exposure using XPS and XRD, monitor mass loss and spallation via SEM, and assess corrosion kinetics through electrochemical impedance spectroscopy.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization curves
XPS and XRD characterization of oxide film composition and thickness
SEM imaging of surface morphology and spallation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant differences in corrosion rate, oxide film stability, or oxide scale integrity are detected between the oxidized and freshly polished Q235 steel samples under high-temperature conditions, or if the controlled oxide layer does not confer improved corrosion resistance relative to the polished samples, then the hypothesis that the native oxide film governs the corrosion protection mechanism in Q235 steel is falsified.

The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. This study aims to test the effect of the elemental stability inherent in HEAs due to the high configurational entropy and/or sluggish diffusion (if any) on the elemental dissolution in the molten salt. Specifically, the study focuses on corrosion performance and thermal stability of the Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 alloy in molten fluoride salt environment. This multi-component alloy with both Mn and Cr which are reactive in molten fluoride salt is well suited to test these hypotheses. This high entropy alloy was exposed to molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours followed by detailed analysis of corrosion in the near-surface regions of the alloy in terms of elemental dissolution into the molten salt and morphological changes at the surface. The results were compared to that of 316 H stainless steel tested under similar conditions.

decision.trend: Earlier studies in high‐temperature corrosion and hot‐corrosion behavior—especially on HEAs and stainless or boiler steels—progressed by modifying alloy microstructures through annealing and controlled processing to induce stable and protective oxide scales. Researchers first characterized the load-bearing and thermal attributes (e.g., phase transformation, precipitation) of these advanced alloys, then correlated observed microstructural changes (such as the formation of Cr‐rich or Al‐rich phases) with improvements in corrosion resistance under aggressive salt environments. However, these works typically emphasized performance metrics and tailored alloy design rather than deconvoluting the intrinsic, mechanistic reasons for protective oxide stability versus failure in untreated materials.
decision.unsolved: For as-received Q235 steel, it remains unclear how its inherent microstructural state—and the nascent oxide layer that develops naturally—governs the switch between protection and degradation in both room-temperature and high-temperature (700–900 °C) salt exposures. In particular, the role of native oxide composition, thickness, and defect structure as a self-healing (or failing) protection mechanism is not isolated, and the temperature-dependent oxidation kinetics that might explain the persistence or breakdown of the protective layer have not been specifically addressed.
decision.lever: Design a study that compares Q235 steel samples with intentionally varied native oxide conditions—such as a freshly polished surface (minimal oxide) versus a pre-formed, controlled oxide layer—to a benchmark alloy (e.g., 304 stainless steel) under both ambient and 700–900 °C salt exposure. The key parameters would include controlled annealing to establish a reproducible oxide layer thickness and composition (monitored by in-situ XRD and XPS), salt composition control (e.g., 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl), and subsequent corrosion rate measurements.
decision.why: This approach directly isolates the influence of the pre-existing oxide/microstructure on corrosion behavior—following the trend from HEA and stainless steel studies that linked controlled microstructural evolution with improved corrosion performance—and addresses the gap by providing a testable mechanistic hypothesis. If the pre-formed oxide on Q235 steel is indeed responsible for protection at high temperatures (and fails under room-temperature conditions due to insufficient kinetic stabilization), the controlled experiment will reveal distinct differences between the polished and oxidized states. A failure of the pre-formed oxide sample to show improved corrosion resistance would falsify the hypothesis.
